A field guide to last-mile robot learning · Sep 2025 – Oct 2026

Climbing the Nines

A pretrained robot policy that works half the time needs more reliable behavior before deployment. Even 99% success needs a declared task scope, quality bar, speed and evaluation protocol. This guide explains how people improve reliability: the hill-climbing methods, the textbook RL ideas under each one, and recent developments since September 2025.

If you read seven things from the past year, read these. Each one is a different way to climb, and together they illustrate several major approaches.

Jul 2026 · Sunday Robotics

Sunday ACT-2 Preview

Sunday's framing of hill climbing: scale pretraining until in-house gains carry over to unseen homes, then climb reliability in-house. Proposes the "Solve" reporting standard.

Pretrains ACT-2 on sensorized human data from Sunday's own capture hardware, then post-trains on repeated in-house Memo runs and recoveries (update rule undisclosed). Laundry: 99.1% over 785 autonomous attempts in unseen homes, one fixed checkpoint, zero per-home adaptation.

Industry loops
Nov 2025 · Physical Intelligence

pi*0.6 / RECAP

Advantage-conditioned retraining of a VLA: a value model tags chunks positive or negative, the model is retrained with its supervised loss on that tag, and at test time it is conditioned on positive (optionally with classifier-free guidance).

Fits a distributional value, binarizes n-step advantages into text conditioning, and supervises the whole flow VLA; CFG is optional. Same-data real laundry: about 2x AWR throughput; success ~96% versus AWR ~91%, PPO ~75% (chart reading).

Advantage-weighted BC
May 2026 · Stanford University

EXPO-FT

Off-policy RL around a VLA with no RL gradient through it: propose chunks, apply a small bounded edit, execute the best under a Q-ensemble. The VLA itself keeps training on its own supervised loss.

Samples 8 pi0.5 chunks, adds a tanh-bounded learned edit to each, runs the argmax-Q of 16; the VLA keeps training on its supervised loss, with human interventions. Real, 8 tasks: SFT 20.5/30 → 30/30 each, 19.1 min average (HG-DAgger 22.1/30).

Off-policy critics
Mar 2026 · Robotics and AI Institute; Arizona State University; Northeastern University

Golden Ticket

Black-box search (random search, CEM, zeroth-order) for one fixed input-noise vector for a frozen diffusion or flow policy, training no new networks. Simple enough to run before RL: it beat Gaussian noise sampling on 46 of 51 sim and real tasks.

Replaces per-chunk Gaussian noise in a frozen diffusion or flow policy with one fixed noise vector found by black-box search. Real Franka block/cube pick: 80 → 98% success on 50 held-out episodes after 150 search episodes (~30 min).

Black-box search
Jun 2026 · University of Washington; Amazon FAR

SCORE

Noise-space steering constrained to what the base policy can already do, trained only in a scanned digital twin, transferred with zero real RL.

Freezes a real-demo flow policy; in a scanned sim twin, PPO learns to steer its input noise plus a small residual, staying near the base's action support. Real Franka/LEAP, 8 tasks, no real-world RL: 37.8% → 89.9% vs Residual-RL 59.5%.

Residual & steering
Mar 2026 · University of Toronto; Google DeepMind; University of Alberta; Harvard University; UT Austin

UF-OPS

Train a verifier on your own evaluation rollouts and rerank N samples at deploy time. No policy weight updates.

Trains a small verifier on labeled evaluation rollouts of the deployed policy, then reranks 10 samples from the frozen diffusion or flow policy. Real ALOHA, 5 tasks, 20 trials each: mean success 38% → 87% (chart reading).

Test-time search
Sep 2026 · Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Xiaomi Robotics

Dissecting advantage-guided post-training

A controlled study of advantage-guided (RECAP-style) post-training that separates how the advantage is built, calibrated and used, screens each choice with offline diagnostics, then tests the recipe on four real bimanual tasks.

Ablates separately how critic-derived advantages are built, calibrated and used; n-step TD, per-value-bin normalization and soft exponential weights on the pi0.5 loss worked best. Real bimanual, 4-task mean success: SFT 0.11, source-weighted DAgger 0.45, continuous weighting 0.74.

The hill-climbing loop

In 2025-26, most last-mile improvement of robot policies can be read as one loop: deploy, measure, find failures, improve, re-measure. The families mostly differ in which step they put effort into and which part of the system they change. Pretrained VLA and BC policies, once fine-tuned on a task, usually start well above zero, so in many recent papers the optimizer is not the main bottleneck. The bottlenecks are the signal (success checks, rewards, advantages, verifiers), trustworthy evaluation, and human and robot time. Many recipes that work keep the large model frozen and climb with something small: a noise vector, a residual or edit head, a critic, a verifier or a curated data slice. Others update the whole model but limit how far it moves: they restart each round from the pretrained checkpoint (RECAP), or keep the supervised loss and change only which data or advantage label it copies. Full-model RL with no KL anchor also works when the starting policy already succeeds often enough (SimpleVLA-RL). Under the new names, the classic ideas of perturb-and-score search and reward-weighted averaging are still there.

Narrative drawn from the linked papers and posts.

step 0

Start

Begin from a pretrained policy that already succeeds sometimes: a BC diffusion or flow policy, ACT, or a VLA such as pi0, pi0.5 or OpenVLA-OFT. If it never succeeds (0%), most methods have nothing to climb: on five RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, SimpleVLA-RL on an OpenVLA-OFT base model given no task demonstrations (0-trajectory SFT) stays at 0% after RL, because every rollout earns zero reward. The exceptions change how they explore instead: PDE has a VLM rewrite the instruction and climbs LIBERO-PRO from a 0% start.

step 1

Deploy

Run the policy to collect episodes. They can come from the real robot, a fleet, a GPU simulator, a scanned or generated digital twin (the sim-to-real family), or a learned action-conditioned video world model (the world-model family). Each has a cost: real episodes need resets and supervision, and simulated ones can be wrong in ways the policy will exploit.

World models & evalSim-to-real
step 2

Measure

Turn each episode into a number. The options are a binary success check (a human keypress, a hand-written detector, a classifier), a dense progress or value model (the reward family), or a VLM judge. For comparing checkpoints, you want an evaluator that ranks policies the same way reality does, reported as Pearson r and MMRV against paired real trials (the world-model/evaluation family). Offline validation action MSE is a poor proxy: when SIMPLER ranked 6 checkpoints on 3 Google Robot tasks, MSE averaged Pearson r 0.308 against real success, vs 0.924 for visual-matching sim.

Rewards & progressWorld models & eval
step 3

Find failures

Locate where and why the policy goes wrong. The tools are dips in a progress model (Dyna), runtime monitors, either calibrated on successful runs (CoRe) or triggered when the critic's Q jumps away from its recent moving average (JITI, which targets lapses in execution quality rather than outright failures), human takeovers (the HITL family), VLM diagnosis of failed videos (F4R, PDE), and per-stage predicates (Temporal GRPO). This step decides where the next batch of data, search or corrections goes.

Rewards & progressHuman corrections
step 4

Improve

Apply an update. Each family is a different update operator:

Black-box searchOn-policy PGOff-policy criticsResidual & steeringAdvantage-weighted BCHuman correctionsTest-time search
step 5

Re-measure

Evaluate on held-out episodes and start states that were not used for search or training. Report trial counts and confidence intervals, and track speed, intervention rate and per-task results, not just average success. Then repeat. Many loops also distill what worked back into the base (PLD, VERITAS); Q-Planning instead refits only its critic each round and leaves the policy frozen. Others restart each round from the pretrained checkpoint to avoid drift (RECAP). Restarting does not fix a skewed data mix, though: DEED, a RECAP adaptation on a humanoid, restarted every round and still fell from 42% (21/50) to 22% (11/50) in round 2 (its round-1 gain over the 32% starting policy was not statistically conclusive); its authors attribute the drop to self-generated rollouts crowding out the teleoperation demos.

World models & evalIndustry loops

The update operators (step 4)

  • Black-box search perturbs a small parameter set (gains, a noise vector, a recipe) and keeps what scores better.
  • On-policy PPO/GRPO raises the log-probability of rollouts that beat a baseline.
  • Off-policy actor-critic learns Q from every stored transition and pushes actions toward higher Q.
  • Residual, edit and steering methods train a small add-on around a frozen base.
  • Advantage-weighted or advantage-conditioned BC keeps the supervised loss but chooses what to copy.
  • DAgger-style methods train on human (or machine) corrections at the states the policy actually reaches.
  • Test-time search leaves the policy's weights unchanged: it samples candidates and picks with a verifier, or guides the sampler with a critic's gradient (the verifier or critic may itself be trained).

Reward and value models serve steps 2-3 for everyone else. World models and twins make steps 1-2 cheap. HITL methods put a person into steps 3-4. Industry recipes are mostly this loop built as infrastructure: fleet logging, auto-grading, targeted retraining.

Measuring the nines

Near the top, the hard part is knowing whether you actually climbed. An evaluation with only 20–50 trials cannot reliably distinguish 95% from 99% success.

30/30

gives a 95% Wilson interval of [88.6%, 100%]. A perfect observed score does not prove perfect reliability.

73/73

successes at a fixed evaluation size give a Wilson interval whose lower bound reaches 95%.

381/381

successes at a fixed evaluation size give a lower bound of 99%. Correlated attempts or changing task conditions need additional analysis.

778/785

Sunday’s laundry result gives a 95% interval of [98.2%, 99.6%]. Sunday’s “Solve” label rests on more than the interval: a declared scope and zero per-home adaptation.

Interval calculator

0%25%50%75%100%

Wilson score interval at 95%, assuming independent trials with a constant success probability and a fixed evaluation size. Report it next to the observed rate, keep search separate from evaluation, and use paired start states when comparing methods.

Which method when

Pick by what you have: how often the base succeeds, whether you have a simulator, how much robot time and human time you can spend, and whether you can touch the weights.

Narrative drawn from the linked papers and posts.

You only have a scalar episode score (e.g. binary success), the policy is a frozen diffusion or flow model, and you want a cheap gain before trying RL.
UseBlack-box random search or CEM over one fixed initial-noise vector (Golden Ticket).
EvidenceThe search space is tiny (28-1600 dims) and needs no log-probs. On a real Franka pick task, success went 80 → 98% on 50 held-out episodes after 150 search episodes (~30 min). It can only select behavior the policy already has, so it is also the baseline any RL method should beat.
You are tuning fewer than about 10 controller knobs (PID/LQR gains, impedance, MPC weights), and each real trial is expensive.
UseBayesian optimization (GP surrogate plus MES for noisy objectives or LogEI for low-noise ones), starting from about d+4 initial points, the review's recommended default.
EvidenceOf 110 hardware BO papers reviewed, 57 use vanilla BO, and the vast majority tune fewer than 10 parameters (Decade of BO for control). The authors place BO in the micro-data regime, where tens of experiments can be enough.
A PPO or SAC policy has plateaued in simulation, and what you are graded on is a trajectory-level metric that does not split into per-step rewards.
UseA black-box 'stage 2' (SNES, TD-ES) that starts from the gradient-trained checkpoint and uses the exact metric as fitness.
EvidenceEvolSAC cut cartpole swing-up time from 2.085 s to 1.135 s, where 1000 more SAC episodes reached only 1.565 s. TD-ES raised aggregate IQM success from 67.2% (PPO) to 85.0% on Isaac Lab Franka tasks (simulation only).
You have a strong SFT VLA (roughly 10-90% success), a parallel simulator with cheap resets and an automatic success check, and 8x 80GB-class GPUs.
UseOn-policy PPO with a critic, or GRPO/RLOO, anchored to the pretrained policy: low actor LR, a BC term, little or no entropy bonus, critic warm-up. For flow VLAs, use Flow-Noise/Flow-SDE or FPO-style ratios.
EvidencepiRL took pi0 from 57.6% to 97.6% on few-shot LIBERO (sim, 8x H100). In the RLinf team's own same-codebase comparisons, PPO beat GRPO each time (piRL Flow-SDE: pi0 96.0 vs 90.0, pi0.5 97.9 vs 91.5; RLinf-VLA ManiSkill ID: OpenVLA 96.09 vs 84.38). ADEPT (sim PPO for a dexterous hand, not a VLA): standard PPO at LR 1e-3 got 0/5 seeds to ADR 50 (all collapsed at ADR 20), while the low-LR recipe got 5/5; adding a KL penalty did not prevent the collapse.
The policy is at or near 0% on the target task.
UseDo not run plain RL or noise steering. Get successes first: prompt exploration (PDE), hindsight relabeling (LfH), human corrections or new demos, or change pretraining (TMRL).
EvidenceWith 0/1 reward and every rollout in a group failing, group-relative advantages (GRPO/RLOO) are exactly zero, and a critic sees no success to learn from. On one LIBERO-PRO task where action-noise PPO stayed at 0% for 120 steps, PDE reached 81.8% (the authors suggest that skills learned from successful exploratory rollouts on related tasks transferred). Noise steering cannot leave the base's support: from a 1-demo BC base at 33.5% on LIBERO-Long (zero-shot 0%), DSRL stays at 33.5 while MiDAS reaches 91.2.
You are on a real robot with a budget of minutes to hours, and the VLA is too large or too costly to backpropagate RL through.
UseOff-policy RL around the frozen or co-trained VLA: an edit policy with argmax-Q selection over proposals (EXPO-FT, Real-Time EXPO-FT), or a small anchored actor on VLA features (RL Token).
EvidenceEXPO-FT took pi0.5 from an average of 20.5/30 to 30/30 on 8 real tasks with an average of 19.1 min of online data. Real-Time EXPO-FT went from 42% to 97% on 4 dynamic tasks within a 10 min data cap.
The base policy is roughly right but imprecise (alignment, contact, force, latency drift).
UseA bounded, zero-initialized additive residual trained with SAC or TD3: 50/50 demo/online replay, a LayerNorm critic on the summed action, and warm-up rollouts from the base policy.
EvidenceResFiT went from 14% to 64% on a real humanoid task after 134 rollouts (~15 min) and was about 200x more sample-efficient than a PPO residual on the sim BoxCleanup task. DAWN finds that seeding replay with base-policy transitions plus critic normalization (such as LayerNorm) fixes the critic cold-start and scale-mismatch problems that slow residual RL.
The base policy already contains the right behavior but picks it unreliably, and you want to improve it in simulation without learning to exploit simulator bugs.
UseLatent-noise steering constrained to the base's support (DSRL, SCORE), or a hybrid of noise steering and a residual (RFS) when a mode switch and a small fix are both needed.
EvidenceSCORE raised real success over 8 dexterous tasks from 37.8 to 89.9 with zero real-world RL, vs 59.5 for residual RL. RFS reports that noise-only and residual-only steering fail in opposite ways.
You have success labels per episode and an existing SFT pipeline, and you want to learn from failures and corrections without RL infrastructure.
UseAdvantage-weighted or advantage-conditioned BC: a value model, n-step advantages, and soft exponential weights or a binary advantage token with CFG. Restart each round from the base checkpoint.
EvidenceAcross 4 real bimanual tasks (20 trials each), Dissecting advantage-guided post-training found continuous weighting at 0.74 success vs 0.50 for hard filtering and 0.45 for DAgger (SFT 0.11). In RECAP's T-shirt/shorts comparison on the same data (read from the chart), RECAP on pi*0.6 reached about 60 successes/hr vs about 30/hr for AWR on pi0.6, at similar success rates (about 96% vs 91%).
Your demos are mixed-quality or contradictory.
UseCurate before climbing: gradient-compatibility or influence scores (RoboDrop, CUPID, QoQ), or cheap smoothness filters.
EvidenceRoboDrop raised average real success from 35.0% to 67.5% just by removing 17-21 of 90 episodes per task (each pool mixed 70 proficient and 20 non-expert demos).
The policy fails in specific, repeatable places, and an operator can recognize and fix them.
UseHG-DAgger with correction reweighting and RaC rules (recover, then correct, then end the episode). Add robot gating or a learned intervention agent once watching time dominates. Switch to takeover-as-signal (RLIF, preference pairs) when the policy should beat the operator.
EvidenceSOP: 3 h of wall-clock fleet interaction with human takeovers took the Base-1/2 model (pretrained on half of ~160 h of data) from 0.571 to 0.800, while 80 more hours of demos took it from 0.576 to 0.612. RaC reached 78.3% on shirt-hanging with 5 h of data.
The policy is stochastic, pass@k is clearly above pass@1, and you cannot or will not retrain it.
UseBest-of-N with a verifier trained on your own evaluation rollouts (UF-OPS, SeeQ), gated so it runs only when samples disagree (VLA-ATTC), or one-step critic-gradient guidance (QGF).
EvidenceUF-OPS raised the real ALOHA mean from about 38% to about 87% with best-of-10 (chart readings; the abstract reports an average 49% improvement over the base policy across 5 real tasks), using a verifier trained on 60 labeled evaluation rollouts per task. SeeQ took pi0.5 from 35.4% to 66.7% on real long-horizon tasks.
Reward is a sparse success bit on a long multi-stage task.
UseA learned progress or value model used as potential-based shaping (gamma*Phi(s') - Phi(s)), not as raw reward, with a held-out ground-truth success check.
EvidenceRobo-Dopamine drops from 85.0% to 41.3% without policy-invariant shaping. RynnValue: real DSRL averaged 72.5% vs 48.8% with sparse reward.
You need to compare many checkpoints and real trials are slow and noisy.
UseA validated stand-in evaluator: a Gaussian-splat simulation rebuilt from a short video scan (PolaRiS) or a learned world model (Veo, RoboWorld). Check its ranking against 5-10 checkpoints with paired real trials before trusting it.
EvidenceVeo eval: MMRV 0.03 and Pearson 0.88 across 8 policy checkpoints in nominal scenes (the paper reports 1600+ real trials in total). PolaRiS: average r = 0.9. RoboWorld: r = 0.989 with the RoboArena leaderboard (8 policies). Learned evaluators often get rankings right but absolute rates wrong.
Real rollouts are the bottleneck, and you have a strong SFT policy plus an action-conditioned world model for your robot.
UseWorld-model RL or filtered BC on imagined rollouts: short branches from real states, refitting on the policy's own failures, reliability weighting.
EvidenceRISE took real pi0.5 from 30-35% to 85-95% with no physical rollouts during the improvement loop (its world model and policy are trained on prior real demos and policy rollouts, and the policy also uses some human corrections). On LIBERO-Long (sim), VLA-MBPO shows full-horizon imagined rollouts falling below the SFT base (52.8 vs 54.6), while 2-chunk branches reach 66.8.
You have a rough simulator of the task, 20-50 real demos and a pretrained VLA, and no budget for real-world RL.
UseBC-anchored sim PPO (sim-real co-training, then PPO plus a real-data BC loss). Then rebuild real failures as twins (F4R).
EvidenceRL-Co took real pi0.5 from 45.9 (SFT co-training) to 66.2 with zero real RL. F4R raised real OOD success from 26.25% to 90.0%, vs 71.25% for budget-matched targeted BC. On one TacCoRL task (Assembly #2), sim RL with no anchor (beta=0) fell below co-training alone in real success (45% vs 55%).
You pretrain a small actor-critic in simulation and can afford 10-60 minutes of on-robot training.
UseThe recipe from “What Matters for Sim-to-Online RL”: keep or warm-start replay, update the actor once per 20 critic steps with actor LR 1e-5, and restore optimizer and target state. Optionally shape with the sim value (SGFT) or seed replay from a twin (TwinRL).
EvidenceIt reports near-perfect Franka vision grasping after about ten minutes of real training. A baseline updating the actor every critic step failed to improve on all robots.

The twelve families

Each family answers one question. For each: where it sits in the loop, the ideas it is built on, when to use it, what changed in the last year, and its must-know works with their headline numbers.

Black-box searchOn-policy PGOff-policy criticsResidual & steeringAdvantage-weighted BCHuman correctionsTest-time searchRewards & progressWorld models & evalSim-to-realIndustry loopsGeneral RL
Loop step · Improve

Black-box search

How do I improve a policy when all I can do is run it and get a score, for example a success flag, and I cannot or do not want to backprop through it?

Treat the policy, or a few knobs around it, as a vector. Try perturbed copies, score each with one number per episode, and move toward the copies that scored well. No backprop through the policy, no critic, no action log-probs.

All 37 entries on GitHub → (23 from Sep 2025 on, 8 must-know) · filter the index

Built on

  • Perturb, evaluate, step (random search / finite differences / ES)
  • Reward-weighted averaging (PoWER, PI2, CEM, MPPI)
  • Adapt the search distribution (CMA-ES)
  • Bayesian optimization (BO)
  • Quality-diversity (MAP-Elites) as a prior
  • Parameter-space vs action-space exploration
  • Black-box search inside modern methods

Use it when

Use it when (1) you only have a scalar, trajectory-level score such as success, success times time, or pass/fail, (2) the policy's log-probs are unavailable or expensive (diffusion, flow, action chunks, deterministic controllers, closed APIs), and (3) you can shrink the search to a small space: controller gains, impedance, a noise vector, a residual or last-layer head, a prompt. Pick BO for tens of expensive real trials over a few knobs.

What changed in 2025–26

The biggest change is scale: evolution strategies went from small networks to full-parameter fine-tuning of billion-parameter models, and Evolution Strategies at Scale (Qiu et al., Sep 2025, ICML 2026) used a population of 30 to beat grid-tuned PPO and GRPO on the Countdown reasoning task for all seven LLMs it tried (0.5B-8B), a language-model result with no robot experiments. EGGROLL (Nov 2025) made large populations cheap, reaching up to 91% of pure batch-inference throughput with low-rank perturbations. On robots the search space got smaller and smarter: the Golden Ticket (Mar 2026) searches for one fixed initial-noise vector for a frozen diffusion or flow policy and improved 46 of 51 simulated and real tasks, while ENPIRE (Jun 2026) has coding agents search over training recipes using real-robot rollouts. Black-box search is also used as a second stage after gradient training, as in EvolSAC and TD-ES.

On-policy policy gradients

How do I take a BC or SFT policy (diffusion, flow, ACT or a 7B VLA) that succeeds 50-90% of the time and push it toward 95-100% using only a success signal, a resettable simulator, and fresh on-policy rollouts?

Roll out the pretrained policy as a stochastic policy, raise the log-probability of rollouts that beat a baseline, and clip each step so the pretrained skill survives.

All 68 entries on GitHub → (56 from Sep 2025 on, 11 must-know) · filter the index

Built on

  • Likelihood-ratio policy gradient
  • Trust region by clipping (PPO)
  • Where the baseline comes from: critic vs group
  • Getting a log-prob out of an expressive policy
  • Anchoring to the pretrained policy
  • Signal needs variance

Use it when

Use it when you have (1) a pretrained policy that already succeeds sometimes, roughly 10-90%, (2) a simulator or digital twin with cheap resets and an automatic success check, and (3) GPUs for large-scale parallel simulated rollouts. It is the right tool for pushing a competent SFT policy past its imitation plateau: in RL4VLA, SFT plateaued at about 16k demos with 0.781 in-distribution success, and PPO reached 0.938 (appendix Table 1). Do not run it directly on a real arm with a small rollout budget; there, prefer the off-policy, residual or human-in-the-loop families.

What changed in 2025–26

A year ago (May to July 2025) the open question was whether PPO or GRPO could train a VLA at all: RIPT-VLA, VLA-RL, RL4VLA and TGRPO showed it could in simulation, while ReinFlow and FPO showed how to run PPO-style updates on flow-matching policies. From September to October 2025 this became standard recipes and infrastructure: SimpleVLA-RL applied critic-free GRPO with binary success rewards to OpenVLA-OFT, πRL made PPO work on the pi0 and pi0.5 flow VLAs, and RLinf-VLA provided shared training infrastructure. With LIBERO close to saturated (several methods report about 97-99% average), 2026 work focuses on where the learning signal comes from, avoiding forgetting, and real-world transfer.

Off-policy critics & offline-to-online RL

How do I take a pretrained robot policy that works 40-80% of the time to 95-100% with minutes-to-hours of real robot data, reusing every demo and rollout I already have?

Learn a Q-function from every transition you have (demos, human corrections, old rollouts, new rollouts), then use it to pick, edit or push the policy's actions toward higher value.

All 122 entries on GitHub → (69 from Sep 2025 on, 12 must-know) · filter the index

Built on

  • Bellman backups and off-policy replay
  • Max-entropy actor-critic (SAC) and its offline-data variant RLPD (the engine of SERL and HIL-SERL)
  • Conservative and in-sample critics
  • The offline-to-online hand-off
  • Action-chunk critics
  • Policy extraction for expressive policies
  • Humans in the loop

Use it when

Use this family when you already have a decent policy (roughly 40-80% on one task), each real episode is expensive, and you can get a binary success signal. Off-policy RL reuses every demo, correction and failed rollout, so it usually needs far fewer robot minutes than on-policy PPO/GRPO.

What changed in 2025–26

The target policy changed: the 2023-24 lineage (RLPD, SERL, HIL-SERL) trained small task-specific SAC policies, while 2026 work wraps the same off-policy machinery around pretrained flow VLAs such as pi0.5 and pi0.6 (EXPO-FT, RL Token, ALOE, LWD, RAPolicy). Critics increasingly score whole action chunks, following Q-chunking (Jul 2025), and follow-ups such as DQC, AQC and ACH decide how long to commit to a chunk. Other work questions how much offline critic pretraining and offline-data replay really help (WSRL, Three Regimes), and the human-in-the-loop HIL-SERL loop is being automated or scaled: AutoSERL replaces the live intervener with a one-demo scripted corrector, and LWD runs the loop on a 16-robot fleet.

Residual, edit & steering policies

How do I push a big imitation, diffusion or VLA policy from 50% to 95%+ when I can't cheaply fine-tune or backprop through it, without breaking what it already does well?

Freeze the big pretrained policy and train a small add-on with RL: one that corrects its actions (residual/edit) or one that picks the noise it is fed (steering).

All 77 entries on GitHub → (68 from Sep 2025 on, 12 must-know) · filter the index

Built on

  • Residual policy: the base is part of the environment
  • Start at base performance: zero-init, bound and scale the correction
  • Off-policy actor-critic with prior data is what makes this fit on a real robot
  • Latent-noise steering: RL picks the noise, not the action
  • Edit policy + best-of-N selection by Q
  • Support versus reach

Use it when

Use it when you already have a decent base (roughly 20-80% success) that you can't or won't fine-tune: a VLA too big to backprop through with RL, a closed checkpoint that allows only forward calls, or a chunked diffusion or ACT policy whose likelihood is awkward for policy gradients. It also fits when you want the base's generality and recovery behaviors kept intact, and when your budget is minutes to hours of real robot time with sparse success labels.

What changed in 2025–26

Over the last 12 months, bases moved from task-specific diffusion or ACT policies to frozen generalist VLAs (pi0, pi0.5, GR00T, SmolVLA, OpenVLA-OFT). Freezing is common because RL through a multi-billion-parameter model is costly, and an untouched base keeps behaviors the new task data never exercise, such as recovery from failure (the case PPS makes for steering a frozen base). Real-robot add-ons are usually trained off-policy (ResFiT, DICE-RL, EXPO-FT, MiDAS); ResFiT reports about 200x the sample efficiency of a PPO residual in simulation. The limits of each branch became clearer: noise steering stays inside the base's support (on one-demo LIBERO-Long, DSRL stays at the BC start's 33.5 while MiDAS's residual actor reaches 91.2), and RFS pairs noise steering for global exploration with a residual for local correction. The EXPO line pairs a large proposer with a small editor and picks the argmax-Q action: Real-Time EXPO-FT reports 42% → 97% on four dynamic real-world tasks with online data capped at 10 minutes.

Advantage-weighted & filtered BC

How do I push a big imitation policy (a diffusion policy or a flow VLA) up on one task using its own rollouts, human corrections and success labels, without running policy-gradient RL through it?

Keep the supervised imitation loss, but decide which actions (or which demos) the policy copies and how much, using a success label, a value function or a data-influence score.

All 61 entries on GitHub → (44 from Sep 2025 on, 12 must-know) · filter the index

Built on

  • Reward- and advantage-weighted regression (RWR/AWR)
  • Filtered BC and rejection sampling
  • Advantage- or return-conditioned policies
  • Classifier-free guidance as a policy-improvement knob
  • Where the advantage comes from
  • Curation: hill-climbing the dataset instead of the loss

Use it when

Use this family when you have a decent BC or VLA policy (roughly 20-60% success) on a specific task, a way to label episodes success or failure, and ideally a teleop device for takeovers, but you do not want to backprop RL through a large flow or diffusion sampler. Start with curation (RoboDrop, QoQ or CUPID-style audits, or cheap smoothness filters) when your demos are mixed-quality.

What changed in 2025–26

The big shift came with pi*0.6/RECAP in November 2025. Advantage-conditioned BC, where the policy is conditioned on a binarized advantage token and classifier-free guidance is optional, suits flow VLAs whose likelihood is awkward to weight, and it joined advantage-weighted BC as a main option; RECAP names CFGRL (May 2025) as the closest prior formulation. In the next ten months at least a dozen groups adopted or adapted the recipe: GigaBrain RAMP, chi0, DexPIE, DEED, ROVE, STEAM, Robo-ValueRL, PACE, DistAL, Facet-0, CLIFT and a prizewinning LeHome Challenge entry (1st in the simulation round, 2nd in the real-world final).

Loop step · Find failures → Improve

Human corrections & DAgger

My imitation policy works most of the time but fails in states the demos never covered. How do I spend a small amount of human time so the next version fixes exactly those failures?

Run the policy, let a person (or now a machine) step in where it goes wrong, and train on those on-policy fixes so the policy learns to handle the states it actually reaches.

All 77 entries on GitHub → (44 from Sep 2025 on, 12 must-know) · filter the index

Built on

  • Compounding error (covariate shift)
  • DAgger: label the learner's own states
  • Human-gated vs robot-gated takeovers
  • Reweighting correction data
  • A takeover as a reward, value or preference signal
  • Human effort is the budget

Use it when

Use this family when you have a decent imitation policy (roughly 30% to 80% success) that fails in specific, repeatable places, and a person who can recognize and fix those failures. It is the default last-mile tool when you have no reward function, when the task is long-horizon or contact-rich, and when you want the policy to stay close to its pretrained behavior.

What changed in 2025–26

Over the last 12 months, the policy being corrected became a VLA: pi0/pi0.5-class models replace small BC-RNNs, and the loops are built as systems. SOP streams fleet corrections to a cloud learner, and HELP splits the human work between a teleoperator and a floor operator who together supervise twelve robots. Methods also get more out of each correction: FlowPRO trains on paired failed and corrected segments with a DPO-style loss, and FlowDAgger maps corrections into a frozen flow policy's noise space instead of retraining it. Machines increasingly take the intervener's role (UniIntervene, Skill-Space Shooting), and how and when a correction is collected is now studied directly (RaC's recover-then-correct rule, TimelyDAgger's takeover timing).

Test-time search & verifiers

My policy sometimes does the right thing but not reliably. Can I raise its success rate without retraining it, just by choosing better among its own samples at run time?

Leave the policy's weights alone and spend extra compute at deployment: sample several candidate actions, score them with a critic, verifier, world model or monitor, and run the best one (or nudge the sampler toward it).

All 133 entries on GitHub → (112 from Sep 2025 on, 12 must-know) · filter the index

Built on

  • Best-of-N with a verifier (sample, score, pick)
  • KL-regularized optimum = guidance
  • Offline critics that are safe to argmax over
  • Lookahead with a model (shooting, MPPI, MCTS)
  • Over-optimization and support
  • Runtime monitors and adaptive compute
  • Search, then distill (expert iteration)

Use it when

Use it when (1) your policy is stochastic (diffusion, flow or sampled tokens) and pass@k is clearly above pass@1, i.e. it sometimes does the right thing, (2) fine-tuning the policy is expensive or risky (a large VLA, a shared checkpoint), and (3) you can afford some extra latency or can batch samples off a shared prefill.

What changed in 2025–26

Verifiers moved from generic to policy-specific: V-GPS (2024) reranked samples with a generic offline-RL Q-function and RoboMonkey (2025-06) with a 7B VLM verifier trained on synthetic preferences, while much 2026 work trains a small critic on the deployed policy's own labeled rollouts (UF-OPS, Q-Planning). For flow policies, gradient guidance started to replace sampling many candidates (QGF, Jun 2026), and gating schemes such as VLA-ATTC and JITI spend extra compute only when it looks useful. Runtime failure monitors became part of the steering loop (CoRe, RL2-VLA). Many of these are single-paper results with few real-robot trials per task, and few methods have been compared head to head.

Reward, value & progress models

My robot only gets a success bit at the end of an episode, or a human has to watch every rollout. How do I get a dense, trustworthy score so RL, filtered BC or advantage conditioning can push the policy from about 60-80% toward 95%+?

These methods leave the policy alone and build the score it climbs against: a learned or zero-shot judge that says how far along a rollout is, whether it succeeded, and where it went wrong.

All 87 entries on GitHub → (60 from Sep 2025 on, 12 must-know) · filter the index

Built on

  • Success classifier as reward
  • Progress from time (time-as-label)
  • Preference and ranking rewards (Bradley-Terry)
  • Potential-based shaping
  • Value model for advantage-weighted updates
  • VLM as a zero-shot judge
  • Reward hacking and pessimism
  • Measuring a reward model before spending robot time

Use it when

Use this family when success is sparse or expensive to judge and the task is long or multi-stage. Examples: cloth folding, insertion sequences, anything where a rollout that gets 80% of the way looks the same as one that fails at once under a success bit.

What changed in 2025–26

Per-task rankers (Rank2Reward) and pretrained visual-embedding rewards (VIP, trained on Ego4D human video) gave way to VLM reward models trained on large pooled datasets: Robo-Dopamine on over 3,400 hours, Robometer on RBM-1M (over 1M trajectories), RynnValue on over 7,000 hours. Training data now deliberately includes real or synthesized failures, so models can score failed rollouts and not only expert ones (RoboReward's counterfactual relabeling of successful episodes, Robometer's trajectory-comparison loss over failed trajectories). Shaping got more careful: Robo-Dopamine feeds progress in through policy-invariant shaping instead of as raw reward. In RECAP-style loops the value model itself became a lever: with the same RECAP pipeline, ViVa reports 80.0% average real success with its value vs 63.3% with a VLM value. The 'No Free Checker' survey notes that how far a policy can be optimized against a learned robot verifier is still largely unstudied, and that no shared benchmark for verifier exploitability exists yet.

World models & evaluation

How do I tell whether checkpoint k+1 really beats checkpoint k, and how do I improve a policy, when every real robot trial is slow, noisy and needs a reset?

Build a stand-in for the real robot, either a learned video or latent world model or a scanned real-to-sim twin, then use it to score checkpoints cheaply and to run the try-score-improve loop without spending robot time.

All 102 entries on GitHub → (91 from Sep 2025 on, 12 must-know) · filter the index

Built on

  • Dyna: learn a model, then practice inside it
  • Latent imagination (PlaNet/Dreamer)
  • Monte Carlo policy evaluation in a stand-in world
  • Model exploitation and compounding error
  • Rewards inside imagination
  • Real-to-sim twins
  • Runtime monitors

Use it when

Use evaluation infrastructure first, almost always. If you will compare more than a handful of checkpoints, build a twin or learned evaluator and validate it on 5-10 checkpoints with paired real trials (report Pearson r and MMRV) before trusting it.

What changed in 2025–26

In the last 12 months the family went from 'world models as evaluators' to 'world models as RL environments for VLAs', and then to 'making those environments trustworthy'. From September to November 2025, World-Env, VLA-RFT and WMPO ran GRPO/PPO-style RL for VLAs inside learned world models, scored by a VLM judge, a learned success classifier or similarity to a reference rollout; the draw was on-policy RL without resets. By February-March 2026 the focus had shifted to hallucination and compounding error: WoVR (keyframe-initialized rollouts, model-policy co-evolution), VLAW and PlayWorld (grounding the model in real policy rollouts or failure-rich play data) and VLA-MBPO (short imagined branches) each target ways an imperfect world model misleads the policy. On real robots, RISE reports 30-35% → 85-95% (20 trials per task) and WoVR 51.1 → 80.0 on a Franka, and evaluators were validated at larger scale (Veo against 1600+ real trials; RoboWorld at r = 0.989 with the RoboArena leaderboard).

Sim-to-real & real-to-sim

How do I get the trial-and-error gains of RL for a robot policy without paying for thousands of risky, hand-reset real-world episodes?

Uses a simulator, often a scanned or generated copy of the real scene, as a safe practice gym where the policy can hill-climb with RL before or alongside a short real-robot stage. Real demos or real replay data keep it tied to reality.

All 46 entries on GitHub → (35 from Sep 2025 on, 12 must-know) · filter the index

Built on

  • Domain randomization
  • Real-to-sim: digital twins and cousins
  • BC-anchored sim RL (sim-real co-training)
  • Sim-to-online RL on the real robot
  • Sim value as a shaping signal
  • Residual correction on a sim-made base
  • Gradient-free and label-light last-mile knobs for frozen policies

Use it when

Use this family when real-world trial and error is slow, unsafe or needs human resets, and you can build a simulator that gets the coarse task structure right: rigid objects, known geometry, a calibratable controller. With a pretrained BC or VLA policy, a few real demos and a rough simulator, run sim RL with a real-data BC anchor (RL-Co, TacCoRL, DLS); for recurring deployment failures, rebuild the failing scenes in simulation (F4R); for a small actor-critic you can run on hardware for minutes, pretrain in sim and continue online. Avoid it for deformables, fluids or contact physics your simulator cannot fake, or when building the twin costs more than collecting real data.

What changed in 2025–26

The simulator changed jobs: earlier sim-to-real trained small policies from scratch and hoped for zero-shot transfer, while now it is also a practice gym for already-pretrained BC and VLA policies, often with real demonstrations kept as a BC anchor during sim RL (RL-Co, Feb 2026; TacCoRL; DLS). Building the simulation got cheaper and more automatic, from phone-scanned twins (TwinRL) to generated 3D scenes (Generative 3D Worlds, Mar 2026), which makes it possible to rebuild only the scenes where the real policy failed (F4R, Sep 2026). Sim-real hybrids also matured: TwinRL runs RL in the twin to seed the real replay buffer, and What Matters for Sim-to-Online RL sets out how to continue sim-pretrained SAC on a real robot.

  • On-policy data aggregation (DAgger and its human-gated variant)
  • Automatic success and progress detection
  • Policy improvement through supervised learning (advantage-weighted or advantage-conditioned BC)
  • Broad pretraining as the reason local hill-climbing transfers (a company claim, e.g. ACT-2)
  • Reliability compounds and evaluation is statistical
  • Sparse outcome reward plus self-play

Use it when

Use these case studies as a template when you have one fixed, economically defined task, a pretrained base policy that already works sometimes (roughly 50-80%), and the ability to run many long evaluation sessions. A common order, pieced together from partial company disclosures: (1) define success with the customer's own quality bar and log everything; (2) automate grading and failure localization (progress model or auto-labeler); (3) collect targeted recovery or correction data where the policy actually fails (DAgger-style); (4) if success plateaus or speed matters, add a value function and advantage-weighted or advantage-conditioned retraining in the RECAP style; (5) report streaks, successes per hour and graded quality over hundreds of trials with a declared scope.

What changed in 2025–26

RL entered industry recipes in supervised-friendly forms: π*0.6/RECAP (Nov 2025) used a value function and advantage-conditioned retraining and outperformed PPO and AWR baselines on laundry folding with π0.6 (a Gemma 3 4B backbone plus an 860M action expert), and Generalist lists learning from experience (RL) among GEN-1's ingredients. Large-scale human data is now presented as what makes post-training cheap: GEN-1 is pretrained on over 500,000 hours of wearable-device data and adapted with about an hour of robot data per task, and Sunday pretrains ACT-2 on sensorized human data. Reporting moved toward production metrics, such as ACT-2's 99.1% success over 785 laundry attempts and Dyna-2's 95 napkins per hour with 93% meeting the quality bar, but these posts give few details of the training updates behind the numbers. A Siemens factory case study is a rare published account of the effort and recurring failure modes of an iterative fine-tuning loop on π0.5.

Broader RL advances that transfer

Which general RL results from the last year change how you should hill-climb a robot policy?

Not robot-manipulation papers: scaling laws for value functions and RL compute, critic and actor-critic design studies, flow/diffusion policy theory, RL for language models (group baselines, off-policy and stale-data training, process rewards, test-time compute), and last-mile RL for driving policies. Robot work keeps borrowing from all of them.

Built on

  • Everything in Foundations

Use it when

Read these when you are choosing an algorithm family or a compute budget, or when a robot paper cites an idea from language-model RL and you want the original.

What changed in 2025–26

RL for language models and RL for robot policies increasingly share a toolkit in 2025-26: critic-free group baselines, KL-anchored fine-tuning from a pretrained model, learned verifiers, and spending compute at test time. Real-robot work still leans heavily on off-policy critics (SAC or TD3 with RLPD-style demo mixing), which language-model RL rarely uses.

How companies climb

What each company says its loop is, the evidence it gives, and what it has not disclosed. Most industry numbers bundle new pretraining with the post-training loop, so none of them isolates how much hill climbing itself contributed.

Narrative drawn from the linked papers and posts.

Physical Intelligence

Recipe

pi*0.6 / RECAP. Deploy the VLA, have humans label every episode success or failure, and let teleoperators intervene (their actions are forced to 'positive'). Fit a distributional value on negative steps-to-success and compute n-step advantages (N=50). Binarize them into an 'Advantage: positive/negative' text token, retrain the whole flow VLA with its supervised loss (token dropped 30% of the time for CFG), and restart each round from the pretrained checkpoint. Also RL Token: a small TD3-style actor-critic on a compressed token from pi0.6 (task-fine-tuned on 1-10 h of demos, then frozen), penalized for straying from the VLA's own chunk.

T-shirt folding, same data, different policy-extraction methods: RECAP about 60/hr and 96% vs AWR about 30/hr and 91% vs PPO about 22/hr and 75% (chart readings; AWR and PPO start from pi0.6, not the offline-RL pi*0.6 checkpoint). Espresso: about 40% after offline RL + SFT → about 92% with RECAP (about 11% for pretrained pi0.6 with no task fine-tuning); the paper reports 13 hours straight of espresso making. RL Token: screw critical-phase success 20% → 65%.

Disclosed / not disclosed

Algorithm, ablation and hyperparameters are published (arXiv 2511.14759). No code. Numbers are mostly bar-chart readings. The text's iteration gains (laundry +50% throughput, box assembly 2x after the second iteration) do not name their reference point, and Fig. 9 shows box assembly first dropping and then improving, so our readings against the initial policy (box about 10 → 13/hr, laundry about 33 → 60/hr) differ from them; treat these readings as approximate. The method relies on human labeling, interventions and resets, which the authors list as a limitation: the system is not fully autonomous.

Dyna Robotics

Recipe

A learned video progress/reward model whose score dips when the robot makes a mistake acts as evaluator, failure finder and data filter. Flagged failure states direct targeted recovery-data collection, then retraining (human-in-the-loop active learning). At customer sites, 'deployment is the eval': fleet-wide logging (>1 TB/day), an auto-labeler that grades each SOP step against the customer's quality bar, human review of new tasks, ambiguous or low-confidence cases, suspected regressions and a sampled slice that checks label quality, and retraining on targeted slices. A separate hardware-health monitor keeps gripper wear from being mistaken for policy regression.

DYNA-1: 850+ napkins in one 24h run with zero interventions at 99.4% success; Dyna reports 98% of folds at grade 3 or above and 75% at its production grade (4-5 of 5). Talk (Jason Ma, posted 2026-09-24): standard post-training stalls near 80%, and the reward-model loop reached 99.4% over 24 hours. Din Tai Fung: 35/hr at 75% quality (Dyna-1) → 95/hr at 93% (Dyna-2). DYNA-1i: about 40 shirts/hour, 20 consecutive failure-free folds per 30-minute window in unseen venues.

Disclosed / not disclosed

No update rule, no reward-model accuracy, no RL objective and no ablation isolating the loop. Dyna credits Dyna-2 gains to pretraining, new capabilities, tooling and systems together. The talk's trial protocol (how many 24h runs stand behind 99.4%) is not stated in its public description.

Generalist AI

Recipe

GEN-1: trained from scratch on 500k+ hours of human wearable interaction data with no robot data in pretraining, then about 1 hour of robot data per task. Five named ingredients: pretraining advances, post-training techniques, learning from experience (RL), multimodal human guidance and inference-time techniques.

99% average on three charted tasks vs 64% for fine-tuned GEN-0 and 19% for training from scratch without pretraining. Box folding in 12.1 s vs about 34 s for GEN-0 and pi0 (folding time only; baseline times taken from their earlier published sources).

Disclosed / not disclosed

Blog only; GEN-1 is offered to early-access partners. No algorithm details and no ablation of GEN-1's own components (the 19% baseline is a from-scratch GEN-0 with no pretraining). No trial counts behind the averages (only consecutive-success streaks, such as over 200 box folds in a row). The 64 → 99 comparison bundles new pretraining, data, compute and algorithms, so the post does not show how much of it comes from RL.

Sunday Robotics

Recipe

ACT-2: pretrain on sensorized human data from Sunday's proprietary capture hardware, then hill-climb reliability in-house on Memo robots. Run repeatedly, surface failures, post-train so the model learns from recoveries. Proposes the 'Solve' reporting standard: performance, declared scope, adaptation cost.

Laundry: 99.1% ± 0.3% SE over 785 attempts in unseen homes with one fixed checkpoint and no per-home adaptation. Generalization gap after identical post-training: 82 points with 0% pretraining, 0 with 100% (50 evals each).

Disclosed / not disclosed

The post-training update rule is undisclosed (deferred to an unpublished technical post). No ablation isolates how much of the 99.1% comes from the hill-climbing loop (the pretraining-scale study holds post-training fixed). Some garment categories have small samples (n=19, n=7).

Figure AI

Recipe

Helix logistics: no RL described. More in-domain demos plus architecture changes aimed at observed failures (stereo, vision memory, state history, force input, a 50% larger decoder).

Over three months, barcode-orientation success went from about 70% to about 95% and handling time from about 5.0 s to 4.05 s. 10h → 60h of demos: 6.84 s / 88.2% → 4.31 s / 94.4%.

Disclosed / not disclosed

Blog only. Ablations appear in a figure with no trial counts or error bars. It serves as the demos-plus-architecture baseline that post-training loops must beat.

Siemens

Recipe

A pure-SFT loop on pi0.5 via OpenPI in a real factory: teleoperate under constraints, hand-review every episode, re-fine-tune the base on all data, evaluate, collect targeted recovery demos, and relax constraints as a curriculum (a 70% gate per round).

2,535 factory episodes (about 10 h) plus about 900 lab episodes. Final success 'did not meet expectations'. In unconstrained trials, 65% of failed episodes left bag contents on the product.

Disclosed / not disclosed

A 5-page deployment case study with named root causes (wrist-camera angle, transparent bags, occlusion, contact). No overall success rate is reported.

AgiBot

Recipe

SOP: 10 robots run pi0.5, humans take over on failure, episodes stream to a cloud learner that publishes new weights every 25 steps (HG-DAgger or RECAP as the loss). LWD: a 16-robot fleet logs everything with sparse success labels, and a learner runs offline-to-online RL (distributional implicit value learning plus adjoint-matching policy extraction) over offline plus fleet data.

SOP+HG-DAgger: Grocery 0.61 → 0.94, Laundry 0.58 → 0.96, Box Assembly 0.70 → 0.98. LWD over 8 real tasks with about 60 fleet robot-hours, averaging binary success on grocery tasks and partial-credit sub-step scores on long-horizon tasks: SFT 0.76 → 0.95 (RECAP 0.85, HG-DAgger 0.85).

Disclosed / not disclosed

arXiv papers with methods. No public code for SOP was found (the project page listed in the paper returned 404 when checked in October 2026). LWD reports its 652.5-hour offline buffer and a roughly 60 robot-hour online budget, but not intervention counts or learner compute. SOP's Fig. 5 and text disagree on one number (0.895 vs 0.800).

Skild AI

Recipe

Physical Self-Play: competitive self-play RL in NVIDIA Isaac Sim (robot soccer; the post gives 'a single objective: score', and opponents are recent versions of the same policy), transferred to a real humanoid. Pitched as post-training to get past the ceiling of human-data pretraining.

140 simulated years of play, then a real humanoid match shown on video. No metrics.

Disclosed / not disclosed

No quantitative results, baselines or algorithm. On rewards, the post gives only the stated objective and says behaviors such as dribbling, shielding and tackling were not hand-rewarded. The post says 'a strong base model like S1' can learn this way but does not state how the soccer policy was initialized; it describes the policy as barely able to walk in its first simulated months.

1X Technologies

Recipe

A learned action-conditioned video world model with a success-value head, used as a repeatable evaluator to rank checkpoints and architectures before real trials. The stated motivation: fully evaluating one humanoid checkpoint in real homes takes days to weeks and hundreds to thousands of trials, while the world model can replay identical starting conditions for every policy.

A technical report states that a world model with 70% alignment picks the better of two checkpoints 15 points apart 90% of the time, and reports alignment rising from 63.06% to 71.17% with cross-task data. The 2024 challenge reports only token-level baselines (GENIE_138M at 8.79 CE loss on its GitHub leaderboard).

Disclosed / not disclosed

A blog plus a 12-page technical report. The report plots world-model scores next to real Arcade task scores for a few checkpoint sweeps and architecture pairs, but gives no trial counts or error bars for the real-world points and no correlation coefficient, and it does not show how the 70% / 15-point / 90% figure was derived.

Classic search, still inside

Perturb-and-score search and reward-weighted averaging did not disappear. Most of it now runs as an inner loop inside newer systems.

Narrative drawn from the linked papers and posts.

  1. Best-of-N with a verifier is one step of random search. You sample N candidates from the policy, score them and keep the argmax. This is the core of IDQL, V-GPS, UF-OPS, SeeQ, CoVer, RoboMonkey and TACO. EXPO-FT and Real-Time EXPO-FT use the same argmax over base and edited proposals, both for acting and inside the TD target (EMaQ-style). QT-Opt picks actions with CEM over a critic, and VLA-ATTC replaces argmax with a knockout tournament.

  2. MPPI/PI2 exponential weighting shows up as 'softmax-Q-weighted averages'. Q-Planning executes a softmax-Q-weighted average of 32-64 proposal chunks, which is one MPPI step. SAILOR does MPPI residual search in a learned world model, and Simulator-in-the-loop cloth refinement runs MPPI in a GPU cloth simulator around the base plan. The Zero-order optimization primer shows MPPI is a natural-gradient step with step size 1/lambda, and that choosing exponential, rank or top-K weights gives MPPI, CMA-ES-like or CEM-like updates.

  3. The KL-regularized closed form pi_ref * exp(A/beta) is reward-weighted regression, and PI2's weights are the same softmax. AWR, CRR, ARFM, IG-RFT and the soft exponential weights of Dissecting advantage-guided post-training use it directly. Filtered BC and rejection sampling (Hi-ORS, SOAR, RoboCat) are RWR with 0/1 weights. RECAP and CFGRL reach pi_ref * p(I|A)^w through an advantage token plus classifier-free guidance. QAM trains a flow toward pi_beta * exp(tau*Q).

  4. ES-style fitness shaping appears in critic-free policy gradients. GRPO's group z-score, (R - mean)/std, is the same normalization ES at Scale applies to population rewards. ARS divides by return std, and OpenAI-ES and TD-ES use centered ranks. The difference is that GRPO perturbs actions per token or step and needs log-probs, while ES perturbs weights once per episode.

  5. Noise-space search is black-box search with the generative policy as the decoder. Golden Ticket runs random search or CEM over one noise vector. Diffusion-ES mutates by re-noising and denoising. DSRL, SCORE, PSS and UniSteer replace search with an RL actor over the same noise space. PSS keeps only the top-k sensitive directions found by finite differences, and INSPO and SDN pick noise without training.

  6. Black-box search at the outer level. ENPIRE runs evolutionary keep-what-works search over whole training recipes on real robots, similar in spirit to Eureka's evolutionary search over reward code, which it cites. Refinery uses a GP plus Bayesian optimization to pick PPO start states. VLA Grounder is compared against the evolutionary prompt optimizer GEPA. CMA-ES-IG learns user preferences from rankings. HandelBot's per-finger refinement is a non-learned, error-driven iterative correction applied before residual RL.

  7. Black-box search as a second stage and for small knobs. EvolSAC runs SNES on the actor weights with the true competition score as fitness after SAC is trained on a shaped reward, and TD-ES continues from a PPO checkpoint with bounded-noise ES once policy-gradient gains become unreliable. BO remains common for small real-world tuning problems: of 110 hardware papers reviewed, 57 use vanilla BO, and most hardware examples tune fewer than 10 parameters (Decade of BO for control).

  8. Shooting and tree search with world models and critics. GPC, IRASim, Latent Policy Steering and DreamSteer rank sampled chunks by predicted outcomes (random shooting). VLA-Reasoner runs MCTS with a frozen VLA as the prior. SVA runs MCTS offline in simulation and distills the returns into a critic that picks among frozen-VLA samples at deployment. tau0-VLA beam-searches over candidate subtasks, scored with a world model and a value model.

Ten lessons

Patterns that show up across families, with the evidence behind each.

Narrative drawn from the linked papers and posts.

These methods mostly select and amplify behavior the base policy already has. They rarely create competence from a zero-success start. Pick your method according to how often the base succeeds.

SimpleVLA-RL: an OpenVLA-OFT base with no task demos scores 0% on five RoboTwin 2.0 tasks and stays at 0% after RL. PDE: on a LIBERO-PRO task where action-noise PPO starts at 0%, action noise, Robometer and RND all stay at 0 for 120 steps; PDE reaches 81.8%; the authors suggest successful exploratory rollouts on related tasks teach transferable skills. From a 1-demo BC base at 33.5% on LIBERO-Long (zero-shot 0%), noise steering (DSRL) stays at 33.5, while MiDAS, which trains a residual actor with value-based RL and reaches actions outside the base's effective support, gets to 91.2. The Golden Ticket paper notes its noise search works only if the frozen policy is steerable. Exceptions exist: ADEPT's RL learned a plate flip-and-regrasp the pretrained policy never succeeded at, and SimpleVLA-RL reports an emergent 'pushcut' strategy.

Freezing or tightly anchoring the big model and training something small is the safer default. Unanchored or aggressive full fine-tuning collapsed or forgot in several studies, though full-model RL can work when the base already succeeds often.

ADEPT (sim, Kuka-Allegro peg task): standard PPO at LR 1e-3 gets 0/5 seeds to ADR 50 (all collapse at ADR 20), while the low-LR recipe gets 5/5. PAC-ACT (sim, sparse-reward ablation): without its KL penalty between successive PPO updates, the policy drifts from the pretrained ACT's trajectories and the final training window drops to 72.7% (22.0% cumulative), vs 100% with it. Simple Recipe Works (continual VLA RL, LIBERO-Spatial): sequential GRPO with LoRA gives AVG 81.2 vs 7.3 with full fine-tuning. FlowDAgger keeps held-out skills at 0.88 (frozen base 0.96) vs 0.02 for SFT. TacCoRL (real Assembly #2): with no real-data anchor (beta=0) it reaches 45%, below co-training alone (55%); beta=0.1 or 1.0 reaches 80%. Counterpoint: SimpleVLA-RL updates all OpenVLA-OFT parameters with GRPO and no KL term and lifts the LIBERO average from 91.0 to 99.1.

The bottleneck has moved from the optimizer to the signal. Holding the learner fixed and changing only the reward, value or weighting often matters more than changing the algorithm.

SARM2: same residual RL from the same checkpoint (4/12 on Shorts Crumpled), and the reward source alone decides whether the loop climbs (SARM2 8/12), plateaus (Robometer-FT 5/12) or regresses (sparse 2/12). ViVa: 80.0% average real success with its value vs 63.3% with a VLM value in the same RECAP pipeline. Dissecting advantage-guided post-training: continuous advantage weights 0.74 vs hard filtering 0.50 mean success over 4 real bimanual tasks. RoboReward: in simulated Robomimic, offline reward accuracy correlates with RL success at r=0.83.

On real robots, off-policy methods that reuse every transition report far less robot time than on-policy methods. On-policy methods dominate where cheap parallel simulation exists.

ResFiT (sim BoxCleanup): 200k vs 40M steps against a PPO residual (about 200x), the only controlled comparison here. EXPO-FT: 30/30 on every task after an average of 19.1 min of online data, starting from a pi0.5 SFT policy. AutoSERL: 50/50 in 8-45 min from one demo (without start-position randomization). For scale only (different tasks and goals, not a controlled comparison): RL-100, which applies a PPO-style objective to iterated offline and then online rollouts, logged about 14 h of data collection per task (about 1.9 h demos, 6.8 h offline-RL rollouts, 5.3 h online), and FPO++ locomotion trains on roughly 147M-197M sim steps (4096 envs x 24 steps x 1500-2000 updates).

On-policy data, meaning the states the current policy actually reaches, beats more offline demos once imitation plateaus.

SOP: 3 h of on-policy interaction took a model from 0.571 to 0.800, while 80 extra hours of offline demos took it from 0.576 to 0.612. RL4VLA (sim): SFT plateaued at 0.781 in-distribution and PPO reached 0.938. PAC-ACT: doubling demos from 800 to 1600 moved BC only from 60% to 66% on Contour, where RL reached 100%. VT-Refine (visuo-tactile, evaluated in sim): going from 30 to 50 demos moved BC only from 0.48 to 0.57, while sim RL from the 30-demo policy reached 0.94; on the real robot, RL raised the visuo-tactile policy from 0.50 to 0.85.

A strong pattern: train on a convenient proxy first, then hill-climb the exact metric in a separate stage.

EvolSAC: SAC on a surrogate reward, then SNES directly on the target score. On the cartpole task, swing-up time fell from 2.085 s to 1.135 s, where 1000 more SAC episodes reached 1.565 s; the same recipe was then applied to the AI Olympics competition score. Q-Planning: on real stack-cups, critic-only rounds on a frozen BC policy go from 40% to 90%, where SFT on successful rollouts stalls at 55%. Related, but without a metric switch: TD-ES refines PPO checkpoints with bounded ES on the same return, lifting IQM success from 67.2% to 85.0% (Gaussian ES: 73.7%) at a fixed total budget.

Learned judges (reward models, world models, preference losses) can be exploited under optimization. Use shaping, anchors, short horizons and an independent success check.

Robo-Dopamine: without its policy-invariant shaping, the raw progress reward drops a 3-task real average from 85.0% to 41.3%. FlowPRO: plain DPO on correction pairs collapses PACK success to 13% from an 80% SFT base. VLA-MBPO: full-horizon world-model rollouts compound model error and fall below SFT on LIBERO-Long (52.8 vs 54.6), while 2-chunk branched rollouts reach 66.8. PlayWorld: a policy fine-tuned inside a world model trained only on human demos peaked at 45% and then fell to 25% on carrot removal, below its 30% base (chart reading, 20 trials per checkpoint). GPT-5 as reward: in the SOLE-R1 authors' review of failed rollouts, 42% of failures come from hallucinated success, vs 9% for SOLE-R1.

Human time is the real budget. When and how a correction is collected changes results as much as how many corrections you collect.

TimelyDAgger (sim OpenDrawer) at a matched expert budget: 42% with immediate takeover vs 78% with takeover at step 80. UniIntervene vs HIL-SERL on 5 real tasks: intervention rate 14.6% vs 34.3%, success 88% vs 81%. PAKT reports 62%-86% fewer cumulative interventions than HIL-SERL. Skill-Space Shooting's machine corrector scored above duration-matched extra human demos on all 4 tasks: clearly on Coffee (71 vs 46 progress) and Sweeping (84 vs 63), narrowly on Stack-3 (0.83 vs 0.80) and Drawer (0.60 vs 0.50), one run each.

Average success hides regressions in speed, behavior modes, individual tasks and task handoffs. Report those too.

RECAP's ablation (laundry, T-shirts and shorts): AWR keeps about 91% success (RECAP about 96%) but about 30/hr vs about 60/hr. BMD (Avoid, 24 modes): residual RL keeps 0.98 success but solves only 1 of 24 modes at 80% or better, vs 20 for the pretrained policy. Uncertainty-gated exploration noise (one small-compute LIBERO-10 study with a 450M SmolVLA): PPO with fixed noise collapsed individual tasks in 2 of 3 seeds and learned noise in every seed, and no arm beat the BC baseline of 0.648. Foresight: residual RL lifts oracle-initialized subtasks to 98.4/92.2/99.2, but the chained full task stays at 54.5% (85.6% with foresight rewards). HELP: round-1 training on recovery data raised Test Tube success from 35% to 55% but slowed execution from 93 s to 105 s, as the policy made extra recovery moves (round 2 reached 95% at 93.4 s).

Small evaluations overstate gains near the ceiling. Separate search from evaluation and report confidence intervals.

EXPO-FT: 30/30 is still consistent with a true success rate of roughly 88-90% at 95% confidence. Golden Ticket: the SimplerEnv 63.0 → 89.5 figure takes the best of 9 tickets by their held-out success (base numbers from NVIDIA's public evaluation), while picking by search reward gives +14.8 points. DEED's round-1 gain (32% → 42%, 50 trials each) has overlapping 95% CIs, as the authors note, and round 2 fell to 22%. R2S-Eval notes that real-world success-rate rankings can change across repeated evaluations, and that policies with similar success rates can differ substantially in execution quality.

Open problems

Narrative drawn from the linked papers and posts.

  • Attribution in headline results: GEN-1, Sunday ACT-2 and Dyna-2 bundle new pretraining with the post-training loop, and none isolates the loop's share of the headline number (Sunday varies pretraining scale under a fixed post-training recipe, not the reverse). From the public posts alone, it is not possible to say how much of a 64 → 99 or 75% → 93% jump comes from hill climbing.
  • The 95-99% regime needs better measurement. With 30/30 successes, a 95% confidence interval still reaches down to about 88%; real-world success-rate rankings can change across repeated evaluations; many results are bar-chart readings or single seeds; and some papers change numbers across arXiv versions or reuse baseline rows from earlier papers. There is no shared, reset-realistic real-robot benchmark with matched budgets and confidence intervals.
  • No matched comparison across families: on-policy vs off-policy vs residual vs advantage-weighted BC vs test-time search vs world-model RL at equal human effort and robot time. Most papers compare against their own starting SFT policy or a few in-family baselines.
  • How far a policy can be optimized against a learned judge before the judge breaks: the 'No Free Checker' survey calls this question largely undeveloped in robotics and finds no shared benchmark for verifier exploitability, and hallucination detectors (HaWMPO, Sword) are only partial.
  • Starting from 0% without humans: PDE and LfH use large VLMs and are shown only in simulation or small real tests. Noise steering and search are capped by the base's support, and no simple test tells a practitioner in advance which regime they are in.
  • PPO vs GRPO and critic vs critic-free: three simulation comparisons favor PPO with a critic (RL4VLA; RLinf-VLA, 96.09 vs 84.38 on ManiSkill; piRL, 96.0 vs 90.0 on LIBERO; the last two come from the same RLinf team), yet widely used VLA recipes such as SimpleVLA-RL are critic-free GRPO. How this depends on policy type, reward density and budget is not understood.
  • Critic pretraining and anchoring: Cal-QL, ConRFT and FORCE say calibrated critic pretraining helps, while WSRL, IPE and Q2RL say naive pretraining adds little. It is also unknown how far bounded edits and L2-anchored actors can move from the base policy.
  • Regression and forgetting across rounds and tasks: DEED dropped from 42% to 22% in round 2; multi-task PPO collapses individual tasks (Uncertainty-gated exploration noise); one study finds that ES fine-tuning of LLMs causes significant forgetting, while a later analysis finds it need not; and only PLD shows a distillation flywheel back into the base at scale.
  • Objectives beyond success: recovery data can slow policies (HELP); in RECAP's policy-extraction ablation, AWR reaches 91% success at about half RECAP's throughput (about 30 vs 60 successes per hour, chart readings); and RL can collapse onto one behavior mode (BMD). Speed, quality and mode coverage are rarely optimized or reported together.
  • Removing the human: value-model and VLM interveners (UniIntervene, Skill-Space Shooting, AutoSERL, FIND) work on specific tasks. Whether they generalize, and what happens when they are confidently wrong, is untested. Most HITL results use one operator.
  • Contact, deformables and tactile sensing remain weak points for both video world models (contact hallucination per PolaRiS) and rigid-body twins. Sim success is only a partial proxy for checkpoint selection: F4R reports a sim-real success correlation of r = 0.7625 across 8 tasks and 24 checkpoints.
  • Whether weight-space ES (ES at Scale, EGGROLL) works on real VLA or diffusion robot policies, where episodes are stochastic and far more expensive than greedy LLM decoding. No robot results exist yet.

Build it yourself

This guide is the map for lastmile, an open-source course in the same repo: one robot, one task, a starting policy that works about half the time (a behavior-cloned flow policy; Chapters 1 and 2 tune a mis-tuned scripted controller instead), and a chapter plan spanning twelve approaches to improvement. Implemented chapters report success and costs in robot-minutes and human-minutes; several approaches remain planned.

A low-cost SO-101 arm (the AgileX PiPER is supported in simulation too) picks up a cube and drops it in a cup. Everything runs in MuJoCo on a laptop without an NVIDIA GPU. Each chapter also describes a real-arm step for the SO-101; none has been run on hardware yet, and each carries a safety note to read first. Published full runs report a Wilson interval on fixed held-out start states, robot-minutes (search, training and evaluation kept separate) and human-minutes. Quick runs use search states for their diagnostic scores.

Benchmark limitation: CupDrop-v1 can count a successful drop after the cup was moved or tipped and recovered. These scores do not establish a no-shoving benchmark; the measurements are in the design contract (§2).

9 of 13 chapters are available. The result column is the headline each chapter leads with, on the held-out set with its 95% Wilson interval: pooled over seeds, or a single run in Chapter 0 (one base) and Chapter 3 (whose method is to pick one ticket on the search set), and never a seed picked by its held-out score. Every seed is scored on the same 256 held-out start states, so a pooled interval, which treats the seeds as independent, is narrower than the evidence supports. The chapter notes have every run and what went wrong.
